name: Project Charter
purpose: The charter formally authorizes a project or a phase. It states why the project exists, describes it at a high level, and names the project manager together with that person's authority level. It is written once and only revised after a significant change in the environment, scope, schedule, resources, budget or stakeholders.

elements.guidance: The reason the project is undertaken. It may point to a business case, the organization's strategic plan, external factors, a contract agreement or any other reason.
A summary-level description of the project.
The limits of the project scope, such as scope exclusions or other limitations.
The high-level project and product deliverables; the project scope statement elaborates them later.

The high-level conditions or capabilities needed to meet the project purpose, including the product features and functions that satisfy stakeholder needs and expectations; the requirements documentation elaborates them later.

An assessment of how risky the project is as a whole, covering political, social, economic and technological volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity. It concerns stakeholder exposure to variation in the project outcome.

elements.element: Project objectives and related success criteria
elements.guidance: Objectives are usually set for at least scope, schedule and cost; the success criteria are the metrics used to judge them. Quality, safety and stakeholder satisfaction objectives may be added. The blank form prints this as one table whose columns are Project Objectives and Success Criteria, with rows Scope, Time, Cost and Other.
Significant events such as completion of key deliverables, the start or end of a phase, or product acceptance. The blank form pairs each milestone with a Due Date.
The funding available for the project; it may include funding sources and annual funding limits.

An initial, high-level list of people or groups who influence or can influence project success, and those influenced by its success; the stakeholder register elaborates it later. The blank form pairs each stakeholder with a Role.
The performance, metrics, conditions or other measurements that must be met to conclude the project.

elements.element: Assigned project manager, responsibility, and authority level
elements.guidance: The project manager's authority over staffing, budget management and variance, technical decisions and conflict resolution. The four sub-fields below carry the detail.
Staffing authority, for example the power to hire, fire, discipline, accept or not accept project staff. This sub-field is described inside the authority row of Table 1.1, not as a row of its own.

elements.element: Project manager authority: budget management and variance
elements.guidance: Budget management is the authority to commit, manage and control project funds; variance is the level of variance that requires escalation. Described inside the authority row of Table 1.1.
The authority to make technical decisions about deliverables or the project approach. Described inside the authority row of Table 1.1.
How far the project manager can resolve conflict within the team, within the organization and with external stakeholders. Described inside the authority row of Table 1.1.

elements.element: Name and authority of the sponsor or other person(s) authorizing the project charter
elements.guidance: The name, position and authority of the person who oversees the project manager for the purposes of the project. Common authority types are approving changes, setting acceptable variance limits, resolving inter-project conflicts and championing the project at senior management level.

tailoring: Combine the charter with the project scope statement, especially for a small project.
When the project is done under contract, the statement of work can serve as the charter in some cases.

decisions.decision: Whether the project or phase is formally authorized, and by whom
decisions.notes: The prose says the charter formally authorizes the project; the Approvals block carries the signatures. The bullet list also names project approval requirements, which the blank form prints only as Approvals.

decisions.decision: Who is the project manager and at what authority level
What variance level has to be escalated to the sponsor
decisions.notes: Variance is defined in the project manager row of Table 1.1 as the level that requires escalation.

decisions.decision: Which authority the sponsor holds, such as approving changes and determining acceptable variance limits
decisions.notes: The book lists these as common types of sponsor authority, not as a fixed list.

decisions.decision: Which conditions let the project be concluded
Which objectives are measured and by which success criteria
